title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ κύων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 36. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ εἰς ἀγέλην προβάτων εἰσελθοῦσα, θηλαζόντων τῶν ἀρνίων ἓν ἀναλαβομένη, προσεποιεῖτο καταφιλεῖν.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx eis agelēn probatōn eiselthousa, thēlazontōn tōn arniōn hen analabomenē, prosepoieito kataphilein.
sentences.l: A fox, having gone into a flock of sheep, the lambs being at suck, having taken one up, made a pretence of kissing it.
sentences.i: A fox got into a flock of sheep and, while the lambs were suckling, picked one up and made a show of kissing it.
sentences.n: προσποιεῖσθαι with the infinitive is “to pretend to be doing” — the verb of every animal in these fables with a design in hand. θηλαζόντων τῶν ἀρνίων can be read two ways: as a genitive absolute, “while the lambs were suckling,” or as a partitive genitive with ἕν, “one of the suckling lambs.” The sense hardly shifts, and Chambry's commas leave it open.

sentences.t: Ἐρωτηθεῖσα δὲ ὑπὸ κυνὸς τί τοῦτο ποιεῖ· « Τιθηνοῦμαι αὐτό, ἔφη, καὶ προσπαίζω. »
sentences.tr: Erōtētheisa de hypo kynos ti touto poiei· « Tithēnoumai auto, ephē, kai prospaizō. »
sentences.l: And being asked by a dog why she was doing this: « I am nursing it, she said, and playing with it. »
sentences.i: A dog asked her why she was doing that. “I am nursing it,” she said, “and playing with it.”
sentences.n: τιθηνοῦμαι is what a nurse does with a baby — the fox claims the role of nanny. In the indirect question the verb keeps the indicative and the tense of the words actually spoken (ποιεῖ), where English shifts to “was doing.” Greek puts ἔφη inside the quotation rather than before it; the guillemets « » are Chambry's.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ κύων ἔφη· « Καὶ νῦν, ἐὰν μὴ ἀφῇς τὸ ἀρνίον ἀφ’ ἑαυτῆς, τὰ κυνῶν σοι προσοίσω. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho kyōn ephē· « Kai nyn, ean mē aphēis to arnion aph’ heautēs, ta kynōn soi prosoisō. »
sentences.l: And the dog said: « And now, if you do not let the lamb go from you, I shall bring the things of dogs upon you. »
sentences.i: And the dog said, “Now then — if you do not put that lamb down, you shall have what a dog has to give.”
sentences.n: τὰ κυνῶν, literally “the things of dogs”: a bare neuter plural article with a genitive is the ordinary Greek shorthand for “what belongs to X,” and here it means the treatment a dog hands out. ἐάν with the aorist subjunctive (ἀφῇς) is the plain future condition, “if you don't let go.”

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα ῥᾳδιουργὸν καὶ μῶρον κλέπτην ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra rhāidiourgon kai mōron kleptēn ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against an unscrupulous man and a foolish thief the story is well timed.
sentences.i: The story suits a rogue and a stupid thief.
sentences.n: A closing shape that names its target rather than stating a rule: πρὸς … ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος, “the story is well aimed at…”. ῥᾳδιουργός is built from ῥᾴδιος, “easy” — one who takes the easy way and is not particular how.
